blocks.x: Introduction:

Citrus spp. belonging to the Rutaceae family, which has over 140 genera and 1,300 species worldwide, contains the genus Citrus, one of the most important families of fruit crops. It is a long-lived perennial that is grown in more than 100 nations. After bananas and apples, citrus is the third most important fruit crop in the world, with an estimated 100 million tons produced on 7.2 million hectares of land. Citrus fruit has a significant macroeconomic impact because it is widely grown in tropical and subtropical countries. Citrus is the second most important fruit crop, with 93.75 million tons produced globally. Brazil, the United States, Spain, Italy, Egypt, Mexico and China are the top producers of citrus. India is the sixth-largest producer of citrus in the world. It is an evergreen that grows best in sandy loam soil that drains well and has a pH of between 6 and 7.

The fruits nutritional and medicinal properties make them extremely significant throughout the world. They can be consumed raw, juiced or added to beverages. Due to their extreme sensitivity to temperature fluctuations, citrus trees thrive in warm climates-roughly 20°C at night and 35°C during the day-for healthy growth and fruit ripening. For best results, they need enough of sunlight-ideally six to seven hours a day. High humidity is detrimental to these plants, especially during flowering, and too much moisture can encourage fungal infections and root-related illnesses factors, such as diseases, insect pests, nutrient deficits, poor cultural practices and sudden weather changes, limit citrus production. Citrus plants are impacted by a number of diseases, including gummosis, citrus canker, citrus tristeza virus, citrus greening and citrus tree decline. These diseases lower output, result in large financial losses, and have an effect on growers, consumers and the industry as a whole.

An integrated strategy that includes the use of disease-free planting material, resistant types, appropriate cultural practices, and prompt application of chemical and biological control techniques is necessary for the effective management of citrus diseases. In order to properly management these diseases and ensure sustainable citrus production, it is crucial to comprehend their nature, symptoms, spread and epidemiological studies.
1. Gummosis

Gummosis is broadly described as a host reaction in which woody plant tissues produce and release gum rich in polysaccharides. It is viewed as a complex physiological process linked to cellular breakdown and

degradation of cell wall materials, resulting in the liberation of soluble compounds that later polymerize into gum. Researchers interpret gummosis as a consequence of disturbed metabolic activity in plants under stress, rather than a specific disease, and it is often studied in connection with structural and biochemical alterations in the affected tissues.
Symptoms:
Symptom development often begins near the soil line; dark water-soaked areas are formed in the bark and a sour smell may occur in wet conditions.

Water-soluble gum exudes from affected tissues and is particularly noticeable in dry weather. 3. Longitudinal cracking of bark, accompanied by profuse gumming, usually is positive evidence of infection. Soil removal around affected trees reveals bark that is water soaked, slimy, reddish-brown, or black in late stages.
Brown necrotic areas can be seen extending to the cambium and wood. Advanced stages of infection will result in yellow, sparse foliage.

6. At later stages, the dead bark dries, shrinks and cracks and patches may fall off, leaving an open canker. 7. Trees may later collapse and die due to the girdling action of the fungal infection. Infected fruits develop a soft brown rot eventually with a characteristic pungent odour.
Causal organism:

Gummosis disease in citrus spp. can be infected by six different species of Phytophthora (Phytophthora parasitica, P. palmivora, P. citrophthora, P. hibernalis, P. syringae, P. cactorum). Out of these two species- Phytophthora parasitica Dast., which is typically found in tropical and subtropical regions and Phytophthora citrophthora are primarily responsible for the greatest losses in fruit yield. According to Ainsworth's (1973) Classification system , Phytophthora species belong to the kingdom Mycota and the division Eumycota. They fall within the subdivision Mastigomycotina and the class Oomycetes. They belong to the order Peronosporales, and the family Pythiaceae within this class and the genus Phytophthora.
Disease cycle:

Under suitable environmental conditions, chlamydospores germinate and produce vegetative hyphae or sporangia which initiate asexual reproduction. Sporangia are also formed by mycelial hyphae in the presence of water (flooding), which is essential for this process. Both pathogens produce papillate sporangia. Sporangia of P. citrophthora are extremely variable in shape; ellipsoid, broadly ovoid, globose, limoniform or extremely distorted (27-65 x 45-90 µm). Sporangia of P. nicotianae are predominantly spherical and average 30-40 x 38- 50 µm. In water, sporangia are usually borne singly or in very loose sympodia of 2-4 sporangia. Zoospores are produced inside these sporangia, and are liberated via the sporangial papilla which dissolves. The reniform zoospores are highly motile.
Epidemiology:

The fungus P. parasitica usually endures adverse conditions in infected root debris. The pathogen produces chlamydospores, which can survive for a long time in the soil, as the decomposing cortex sheds. These chlamydospores germinate either directly to make mycelium or indirectly to produce sporangia and zoospores when favourable conditions return. Oospores may also form if both mating kinds are present, increasing the fungus's chances of survival.

Wounds are susceptible to infection for up to two weeks, and the area surrounding the base of the trunk must be sufficiently wet. However, foot rot lesions typically do not produce further inoculum, making them of little epidemiological significance.

Citrus orchards frequently include Phytophthora species, however under some circumstances, disease outbreaks can still happen. The disease may spread quickly and result plant epidemics when it is first introduced into a grove or nursery. Brown rot and foliage blight epidemics are more common, particularly in extremely vulnerable hosts like lemons. Propagules sprayed from the soil can infect fruits and young leaves under favourable conditions. Secondary spread occurs through rain splash or wind-driven rain. This kind of dissemination is more common in species like P. citrophthora, which produce a lot of sporangia on fruit and leaf surfaces, than in P. parasitica, which seldom ever produces aerial sporangia. In areas where these species are present and where there is prolonged winter precipitation, brown rot is especially common.
Disease Management:

Using budwood or saplings that are resistant or tolerant to Phytophthora is a crucial tactic to stop the disease from spreading to new places because it is soil-borne. To provide planting material free of disease, the "Budwood Certification Programme," which entails testing, monitoring, and finding resistant mother plants, must be strengthened. In order to raise healthy seedlings, certain resistant plants should be reproduced and given to nurseries.

To stop contaminated budwood and planting material from spreading to new planting locations, strict quarantine regulations must be adhered to. Seed-borne infections can be eradicated by treating seeds with hot water at 48.9°C for four to ten minutes. Furthermore, Phytophthora propagules have been successfully eliminated by infusing electrolytically produced chlorine into citrus micro-irrigation systems. One crucial strategy for treating root, foot, and stem infections is the adoption of resistant rootstocks. In order to create better hybrid rootstocks, breeding programs can also make use of resistant citrus types and related species.

Disease incidence can be considerably decreased by cultural activities such removing diseased or dead trees, performing yearly inspections (including roots), planting trees on raised soil and avoiding injuries close to the base of the trunk.
Maintaining a soil barrier approximately 50cm from the base is also crucial to preventing irrigation water from contacting the trunk.
Furthermore, fungicides such as Subdue MAXX, Chipco Aliette, Banrot and Truban can be applied effectively for managing Phytophthora root rot diseases.
2. Citrus Canker:

Citrus canker is a serious bacterial disease that affects plants in the genus Citrus and is well-known for having a significant influence on citrus crop quality and yield worldwide. According to scientific literature, it is a very detrimental condition that lowers the market value of product and diminishes plant health, causing significant financial losses in citrus-producing countries.

Due to the disease's capacity to spread swiftly, endure in favourable climatic circumstances and interfere with international trade through stringent quarantine regulations, it has been thoroughly studied.
Symptoms:

Every part of the plant that is above ground may exhibit canker symptoms. The formation of eruptive, cork-like, elevated pustules on leaves, fruits and twigs which serve as sources of bacterial inoculum is the primary way to identify them. As a reaction to the illness, infected plants frequently exhibit fruit drop and defoliation. Young tissues are typically more vulnerable to citrus canker than adult tissues because each flush occurs about three times a year.
1. Leaf lesions:

The bacteria usually enters host tissues through wounds, hydathodes, stomata, and lenticels. The first signs are round, greasy, tan, brown or grey lesions that range in diameter from 2-10 mm. The number of infection cycles, the host's sensitivity, and favourable environmental factors-specifically, the presence of a water layer and temperatures between 20 and 30°C all affect the size and severity of these lesions. The canker lesions start to show on both leaf tissue surfaces 4-7 days after infection. It can take longer than 60 days for symptoms to appear under ideal circumstances.
Small, water-soaked patches become visible lesions when the disease worsens due to host cell growth (hypertrophy) and accelerated cell division (hyperplasia).
Usually encircled by a yellow halo, these lesions eventually develop into slightly elevated, blister-like forms that are readily visible under transmitted light.
2. Fruit lesions:
Fruit remain susceptible to infection about for about 90-120days particularly when they are 2.0-6.0mm in diameter although this varies with the citrus species.
In the early stages, lesions resemble enlarged oily glands on the peel, but they gradually darken and develop a corky texture.
These lesions are typically circular and may appear singly or in clusters, often resulting in premature fruit drop.
3. Twig lesions:

Twig lesions typically appear after fruits and leaves have experienced one or more rounds of infection. Fruit lesions and twig lesions have similar symptoms, however twig lesions are not encircled by chlorosis. The bacterium is endemic and spreads through lesions on immature branches.

In these infected tissues, Xanthomonas axonopodis sub sp. citri can endure for a long time. Unless severe girdling infections eventually cause twig death, the elevated, corky sores on twigs may last for several years. Defoliation, dieback, early fruit drop and general tree decline can result from a severe infection by the disease, rendering the impacted fruits less value or unfit for sale.
Causal organism- Xanthomonas citri sub sp. citri

It belongs to the phylum Pseudomonadota (previously Proteobacteria) and the kingdom Bacteria. It is a Gram-negative bacterium. It is a member of the family Lysobacteraceae, the order Lysobacterales and the class Gammaproteobacteria. It is particularly recognized as citri at the subspecies level within the genus Xanthomonas.
Disease cycle:

By rupturing the leaf epidermis, causing cell hyperplasia and colonizing the apoplast, the bacterium infects the host. It grows quickly under favourable conditions, growing within each lesion by three to four log units. Within five days, bacterial cells might leave through stomatal holes and act as a fresh inoculum, allowing the disease to spread.

Bacterial cells can seep out of lesions when there is at least 20 minutes of free moisture, which is necessary for successful infection and lesion formation. During infection, one or two bacterial cells are discharged through stomata as a result of water buildup. The initial six weeks of plant growth are when most infections happen on stems and leaves and the first ninety days following petal fall are crucial for fruit infection. Small, less obvious pustules are typically the result of infections that emerge after this time. Lesions of different sizes are frequently seen on the surface of the same fruit after bacterial infection because fruits are typically more vulnerable to the disease than leaves.
Epidemiology:

Canker-infected branches, leaves, and twigs are the main sources of inoculum. Cankers on twigs and branches, which serve as the primary source of infection, are the primary way that the illness spreads from one season to the next. Although the bacteria in lesions on fruits and leaves survive until these portions fall off, diseased leaves are typically not regarded as significant sources of primary inoculum because they drop early. However, research has indicated that the bacteria can live for up to six months in contaminated leaves. The pathogen may live for 11-12 days in dry settings at 30°C, but only around 9 days in unsterilized soil. It can survive for roughly 52 days in sterilized soil. The bacteria can persist on non-citrus weeds, grasses, and soil and it can exist epiphytically in low populations on citrus plants without exhibiting symptoms. However, in the absence of plant matter or debris, it cannot thrive saprophytically in soil. In general, the pathogen has very little chance of surviving in subtropical soil. Whether exposed to sunlight or shade, it can only survive for 24-72 hours on inert surfaces like cloth, metal, plastic, and treated wood. Additionally, within one to two months after infected leaves or fruits fall to the ground, bacterial populations decrease to undetectable levels due to competition and hostility from other microorganisms.
Disease Management:

Complete eradication is frequently the best course of action when a disease is uncommon in a given area. A quarantine is imposed on affected locations, and eradication operations may last up to a year, with inspections carried out at least twice a year.

Before the arrival of the monsoon, regularly pruning infected twigs and applying Bordeaux mixture@ 1% has been found to be highly effective in controlling the disease. Bordeaux mixture, which contains copper, also helps prevent secondary infections by protecting the pruning wounds from pathogen entry. In recent times, however, nanoparticles have shown greater effectiveness compared to conventional bactericides, whether used alone or combined with them.

Citrus canker has been managed with a variety of chemical treatments, including Ultrasulphur, Perenox, and blends like Blitox with nickel chloride and sodium arsenate with copper sulphate. Glycerin spray @ 1.0% and streptomycin sulphate @500-1000 ppm have been used to treat canker in acid lime.
Additionally, it has been shown that applying six sprays of 1000 ppm streptomycin after two pruning cycles can effectively lower the incidence of illness.

Strong antagonistic activity against CC has been shown by some bacterial strains isolated from the citrus phylloplane, including Bacillus subtilis, Pseudomonas syringae, Pseudomonas fluorescens and Erwinia herbicola.
3. Citrus Tristeza Disease:

In many citrus-growing countries, citrus tristeza disease is a significant and pervasive issue that negatively impacts orchard longevity and productivity. Once established, it is difficult to control because it spreads quickly through contaminated propagative material and insect vectors. Globally, the disease has severely damaged citrus groves, causing enormous financial losses. Growers are forced to replant orchards and make costly management investments since it reduces yield and total farm income. Shortened orchard life and the requirement for certified healthy planting stock result in further losses. As a result, it is regarded as one of the citrus diseases with the greatest economic significance.
Symptoms:

Citrus and Fortunella species are the natural hosts of the Citrus Tristeza Virus (CTV). However, in experimental settings, the virus can also spread to other citrus relatives and some non-citrus plants via mechanical inoculation and aphid vectors.

Stem pitting in grapefruit, pomelo, lime, and some sweet orange cultivars, regardless of the rootstock, and rapid decline in some citrus scion-especially sweet oranges grafted onto sour orange (Citrus aurantium) rootstock-are two key economically significant illnesses linked to CTV.

The virus induces necrosis of the phloem tissue in the bark of the sour orange rootstock, immediately below the bud union with the scion, which is why there is a drop. The transfer of carbohydrates from the canopy to the roots is hampered by this damage.
As a result, the plant eventually runs out of energy and is unable to grow new fibrous roots, which causes the current root system to gradually deteriorate.
In addition to leaf drop, twig dieback, chlorosis and light fruits of lower market quality, infected plants usually have scant foliage that appears dull green to yellow.

Young sour orange, grapefruit, and lemon plants may also exhibit another symptom, called seedling yellows, primarily in experimental settings. Infected seedlings exhibit significant yellowing of their leaves and stunted development.
Causal organism- Citrus tristeza virus (CTV)

It belongs to the phylum Kitrinoviricota and the kingdom Orthornavirae. It belongs to the order Martellivirales and the class Alsuviricetes within this phylum. The virus is a member of the Closteroviridae family, which is distinguished by filamentous particles and large, non-segmented, positive-sense RNA genomes. It is the type species of the genus Closterovirus at lower taxonomic levels. Formally known as Closterovirus tristezae, CTV stands out for its complex molecular biology and capacity to generate a variety of disease symptoms in different Citrus species, including rapid decline and stem pitting.

Numerous aphid species transmit the citrus tristeza virus (CTV) in a non-circulative, semi-persistent way. The most efficient vector is the brown citrus aphid (Toxoptera citricida) The virus can spread quickly in regions where this aphid is established, frequently resulting in almost total infection within a few years of its introduction.

Even though it is less effective, the cotton aphid (Aphis gossypii) nevertheless has a big impact, particularly in the Mediterranean and some regions of North America, where it helps propagate strains that lead to citrus plant loss.
ii) Acquisition and Inoculation:

Citrus tristeza virus (CTV) is acquired by aphids after 30 to 60 minutes of feeding. They can disseminate the virus quickly inside a grove and to neighboring orchards for 24 to 48 hours after acquisition.
2. i) Anthropogenic Dispersal (Grafting):

Human activity, particularly the transportation of infected budwood used in grafting, is the primary cause of CTV's long-distance and transcontinental transmission. In the past, the virus spread to nearly every citrus-growing location due to worldwide citrus trade and the lack of certified virus-free planting material. Since CTV is not transferred by seeds like many other plant viruses, using clean nursery stock is essential to preventing its spread.
ii) Grafting or anthropogenic dispersal:

Human activity, particularly the transportation of infected budwood used in grafting, is the primary cause of CTV's long-distance and transcontinental transmission. In the past, the virus spread to nearly every citrus-growing location due to worldwide citrus trade and the lack of certified virus-free planting material. Since CTV is not transferred by seeds like many other plant viruses, using clean nursery stock is essential to preventing its spread.
3. Host-pathogen interactions and disease symptoms:
The genetic composition of the host is intimately related to the epidemiology of Citrus tristeza virus (CTV). Three main illness syndromes are how the virus manifests itself:

Rapid Decline- This happens when grafting grapefruit or sweet orange scions onto the rootstock of sour oranges (Citrus aurantium). The virus causes necrosis at the graft union, which prevents photosynthates from reaching the roots and causes the tree to deteriorate quickly.

Stem Pitting- Regardless of the rootstock utilized, severe strains of CTV target the woody tissues of the tree. Particularly in crops like grapefruit and lime, this leads to stunted development and low-quality, unmarketable fruit.
Yellow Seedlings- This morphology is frequently employed as a diagnostic sign of infection and is mostly seen in controlled greenhouse circumstances, especially in lemon and sour orange seedlings.
4. Factors affecting the spread of epidemics:

Pressure of the inoculum- Aphid vectors that disseminate the virus find a home in surrounding abandoned orchards or sick citrus plants in residential neighbourhoods, which serves as a constant source of infection. Diversity of strains- There are several strains of the citrus tristeza virus (CTV), including T36, T30, VT and RB. The efficacy of cross-protection strategies is greatly impacted by a phenomena called superinfection exclusion, in which infection by one strain stops the creation of another.

Conditions of the environment- Both aphid activity and viral growth within the plant are significantly influenced by temperature. The temperature range of 20 to 25°C is when aphid movement is most active, which coincides with times of enhanced viral transmission and disease spread.
Disease Management:

Using virus-free budwood from accredited nurseries is the most crucial preventive measure since it helps prevent the virus from being initially introduced during grafting. To guarantee that planting material stays free of illness, stringent quarantine laws and an appropriate budwood certification and registration system are also crucial.

Tolerant rootstocks must be used such as - Poncirus trifoliata, Carrizo citrange, Troyer citrange, Swingle citrumelo and Rangpur lime. These choices increase orchard survival and lower the chance of deterioration. The best method for controlling stem pitting (SP) strains, which can harm citrus trees regardless of the rootstock used, is modest strain cross-protection or pre-immunization.

Applying insecticides on a regular basis in nurseries and young orchards helps prevent the transmission of the virus by lowering populations of aphid vectors like the cotton aphid and the brown citrus aphid.
4. Citrus exocortis or scalybutt:

Citrus exocortis also known as Scalybutt, is a graft-transmissible illness that has a major impact on citrus output worldwide and affects members of the genus Citrus. According to scientific literature, it is a disease that mostly affects vulnerable rootstocks and interferes with normal plant growth and development. The disease's impact on citrus tree longevity and productivity, particularly in commercial orchards, has prompted much research. It is a significant topic in research on certification systems and the use of disease-free planting material since it is frequently discussed in terms of its spread through vegetative propagation and its impact on interactions between rootstock and scion.
Symptoms:
The bark behind the graft union becomes dry, splits and sheds in thin, narrow flakes, which is one of the most obvious symptoms.

Affected trees exhibit a noticeable lack of vigor and are typically much smaller than healthy ones. In sensitive rootstocks like trifoliate orange and Rangpur lime, yellowish patches may appear on the stems. In places where the bark is loose or peeling, tiny drops of gum may be visible.
The smaller trees result in a significant drop in total fruit production, even if the fruit quality usually stays the same.
Causal Organism - Citrus exocortis viroid (CEVd)

CEVd belongs to the phylum Cressdnaviricota and the kingdom Heunggongvirae. It is a single-stranded, circular RNA. CEVd is a member of the Pospiviroidae family, which has a rod-like secondary structure with a central conserved region (CCR) and replicates in the host cell nucleus using an asymmetric rolling-circle mechanism. It belongs to the genus Pospiviroid within this family. Its distinct nucleotide sequence and ability to produce exocortis disease, which is characterized by bark scaling in sensitive citrus rootstocks, set it apart from related viroids like Potato spindle tuber viroid (PSTVd).
Transmission and Dispersal Mechanism:

Citrus exocortis viroid (CEVd) mostly spreads through human activity, particularly through mechanical and vegetative propagation. Unlike many citrus viruses, it is not transmitted by insects. Principal transmission modes involves the following:

Vegetative Propagation-The most used spreading technique in the world is vegetative propagation. Using contaminated budwood for grafting or budding onto susceptible rootstocks (like trifoliate orange) readily spreads the viroid because CEVd affects the entire plant system.

Mechanical Transmission-For up to eight days, CEVd can survive on contaminated instruments such as big branch cutters, pruners and pruning shears. Therefore, routine orchard activities like pruning, hedging, and harvesting may contribute to its spread.
Natural Root Grafting-When nearby roots organically unite, the viroid can also transfer from one tree to another in densely planted orchards.
Dispersal Mechanism:
Contaminated Tools: When pruning and harvesting workers move unsterilized equipment, they may unintentionally disseminate the viroid.

Agricultural Trade: The commercial transfer of diseased planting material, such as germplasm and other propagative parts, across nations and regions is the primary means of long-distance dissemination. Biological Dispersal: Some living entities can facilitate its dissemination even while insects are not involved: Goats: By rubbing their horns against diseased bark and subsequently coming into contact with healthy trees, they can spread the viroid.
Dodder: This parasitic plant (Cuscuta sp.) can facilitate transmission between host plants by acting as a connecting bridge.
Disease Management:

Using only certified, viroid-free planting material is the most crucial preventive precaution. Strict budwood certification processes, which use sensitive diagnostic techniques like RT-PCR to verify that the propagation material is free from infection, guarantee this.

To prevent the viroid from spreading through contaminated sap, running shears, grafting knives, and other equipment should be cleaned after each use on a separate plant. As long as the instruments stay in touch with a 10% bleach (sodium hypochlorite) solution for at least 60 seconds to render the viroid inactive, it is generally considered to be quite effective.

If a plant is found to be infected, it should be entirely removed along with its root system and then destroyed. Disposal methods such as burning, deep burial, or processing at designated composting facilities help prevent the viroid from spreading further.
In high-risk locations, routine testing and surveillance, such as real-time RT-PCR, aid in the early detection of infections before symptoms spread.

Care should be taken when handling and discarding plant debris and citrus fruit trash. Agricultural fields shouldn't be contaminated with fresh garbage from contaminated areas since this could lead to cross-host transmission.
5. Citrus Greening or Huanglongbing (HLB) or Yellow Shoot Disease:

One of the most serious diseases affecting plants in the genus Citrus is citrus greening, commonly known as Huanglongbing (HLB), which is a significant obstacle to citrus output worldwide. It is characterized in plant pathology literature as a systemic disease that drastically lowers citrus orchard sustainability and productivity. Due to its rapid geographic spread, lengthy latent phase, and detrimental effects on fruit productivity and orchard health, this disease has garnered a lot of study interest. Studies on disease control strategies, its dissemination in agricultural ecosystems, and integrated management strategies to reduce its negative effects on agriculture and the economy frequently look at it.
Symptoms:

An irregular, uneven yellowing of the leaves that crosses the veins is the most distinctive symptom. This mottling is uneven on both sides of the leaf, in contrast to nutritional deficits, which typically show up symmetrically along the midrib.
The disease is often referred to as "yellow dragon," infected trees may sprout one or more vivid yellow shoots beneath an otherwise green canopy.

Thick, elevated, and corky veins, particularly on the underside, can be seen in older leaves. Young leaves that are tiny, erect, and chlorotic (yellow or pale) frequently resemble zinc or iron deficiencies. As the illness worsens, trees show signs of stunted growth, thinned foliage, twig dieback, and general stunting. Causal Organism- Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus’ (CLas)

The bacteria belongs to the phylum Pseudomonadota (formerly known as Proteobacteria) and the kingdom Bacteria. Although some sources place it under Phyllobacteriaceae, it belongs to the class Alphaproteobacteria, the order Hyphomicrobiales (previously Rhizobiales), and the family Rhizobiaceae. The organism is a member of the Candidatus Liberibacter genus.
Disease Cycle:

When an infected Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri) feeds on the phloem of a healthy citrus plant, it introduces Candidatus liberibacter bacteria through its saliva, initiating the complicated, circulative and propagative disease cycle of Citrus Greening (Huanglongbing, HLB). Once inside the plant, the bacteria moved from immature shoots to the roots, spreading throughout the vascular system. Notably, research indicates that before any obvious leaf problems manifest, up to 40–50% of the fibrous root system may be lost. Bacteria cause a long-lasting immunological reaction as they infect the plant. Callose deposits are created as a result, obstructing the phloem and interfering with the movement of nutrients and carbohydrates. The tree may appear healthy yet serves as a covert source of infection during the disease's protracted latent phase, which can last months or even years. Yellow shoots and other signs appear over time, leading to broad canopy reduction and dieback.

When uninfected psyllids, particularly the more productive nymph stages, consume diseased plants and pick up the bacterium, the cycle is perpetuated. The infection grows inside the insect's midgut before traveling to the salivary glands via the haemolymph. The psyllid can disseminate the infection to new plants once the bacterial levels are high enough, which continues the decline and spread of citrus orchards.
Epidemiology:

Primary infection, where infectious psyllids enter from outside sources, is the primary cause of the disease's initial transmission. On the other hand, roguing -the quick removal of sick trees-is typically used to control secondary infection, which is the spread of the virus from one tree to another within the orchard.
Disease Management:
To reduce the chance of first infection, always start with certified, disease-free nursery stock raised in psyllid-proof screenhouses.

Check trees frequently for indications like asymmetrical blotchy mottling, and remove diseased (or "hot") trees right away. It can be essential to remove entire blocks from orchards with extreme infection levels (upto 30%).
Intercropping with guava leaves because they naturally exude repellant substances, growing citrus alongside guava may help reduce psyllid populations.

Citrus trees are grown inside sophisticated screened structures that physically prevent Asian citrus psyllids from entering under the CUPS (Citrus Under Protective Screen) system. Despite the high initial and ongoing expenses, it has shown nearly total efficacy in preventing HLB infection.

Applying balanced foliar nutrients like zinc, manganese, and boron can help maintain the productivity of afflicted trees by counteracting nutrient uptake issues brought on by the pathogen's root damage, even though it does not cure the disease.
